abstract: Organic hydrogels are increasingly used in biofabrication, soft robotics, and biomedical devices due to their tunable mechanical properties, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and flexible fabrication modalities, including embedded 3D printing. However, both polymer chemistry and fabrication conditions can introduce substantial variability in material behavior, particularly for biologically-derived polymers whose inconsistent molecular composition and cross-linking response affect viscoelastic performance. This variability complicates design, reduces reproducibility, and obscures the steady-state mechanical properties required for functional deployment. In this work, we present an experimental-computational framework for characterizing and predicting the mechanical behavior of 3D-printed hydrogels. The workflow characterizes material behavior across molecular, bulk, and population scales. First, we quantify intrinsic polymer variability via $^1$H-NMR spectroscopy to assess monomer distributions governing ionic cross-linking, establishing a molecular-level explanation for observed material variability. Next, we systematically measure how cross-linking time and temperature influence dynamic swelling and stiffness, highlighting representative conditions under which the material approaches steady-state mechanics while maintaining geometric fidelity. Finally, we develop a generative population model to describe geometry and stiffness evolution during cross-linking and calibrate its parameters using Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods, enabling prediction of population-level distributions and variability from limited experimental data. We demonstrate this framework using FRESH-printed sodium alginate constructs as a case study; alginate hydrogels approach steady-state swelling and stiffness after extended cross-linking (>8 hr), and elevated temperatures increase contraction without improving modulus, indicating that low-temperature, long-duration cross-linking enhances geometric and mechanical stability. By integrating molecular composition, fabrication-dependent variability, and dynamic cross-linking behavior into a probabilistic model, this framework provides a structured approach for researchers to quantify uncertainty and design around variability in organic hydrogels, supporting more predictable deployment of soft robotic actuators, tissue-mimetic constructs, and biodegradable devices.
